A robust design treats the search engine as a derived, eventually consistent projection, never as the authorization source or source of truth. PostgreSQL remains authoritative for visibility and correctness; Meilisearch is an optional accelerator whose async task model must be reconciled rather than assumed complete.

## A. Query and authorization path

Use a SearchAdapter contract with two implementations:
PostgreSQL full-text search is built around tsvector @@ tsquery; it is a viable fallback, but not feature-identical to a dedicated engine. Meilisearch indexing/search capabilities differ materially, so the API should expose only the portable subset unless it explicitly declares an enhanced-engine capability.
Security invariant: obtain candidate IDs, then issue the current SQL query that applies tenant, membership, ACL, soft-delete, publication, and temporal predicates. Return only those authorized rows. Calculate total, facets, snippets/highlights, and “next page” from the authorized result set—not from Meilisearch’s raw hit metadata. PostgreSQL RLS can enforce row visibility and uses default-deny when enabled with no applicable policy; policy expressions are evaluated before user query conditions/functions. This is defense in depth: application predicates remain useful, but database-enforced authorization reduces accidental bypasses.
Bound retrieval, e.g. request at most K=100K = 100K=100 candidate IDs for a 20-item response, authorize them, and optionally make one bounded refill request. If filtering leaves too few authorized records, return a partial page rather than unbounded scanning. Use opaque cursors carrying a query fingerprint, engine generation, last score/tie-breaker, and expiry; do not expose offset-driven “page 10,000” semantics.

## B. Durable indexing and recovery

Within the same PostgreSQL transaction that changes a searchable entity, write:
- The business row/version.
- An index_dirty projection marker or an outbox event containing aggregate ID, operation (upsert/delete), source version, payload/version reference, index generation, and idempotency key.
That is the transactional-outbox pattern: persist the business update and event in one transaction, then let a separate relay/worker deliver it. It avoids the database-plus-network dual-write gap.
The worker must persist the external task receipt—provider task UID, request/idempotency key, attempted source version, status, timestamps, retry state—before considering delivery complete. Meilisearch document writes, deletes, index creation/deletion, settings changes, and index swaps are asynchronous: requests enqueue tasks and return task IDs; task status must be observed as succeeded or failed.

## Reconciliation rules

- Stale upserts: worker loads the canonical row and compares source version. Superseded events are skipped/coalesced; the newest canonical state wins.
- Deletes: tombstone/version the canonical record or retain an outbox delete until observed successful. Never let an old upsert revive a deleted document.
- Unknown external completion: after timeout/crash, do not blindly replay. First inspect the stored task receipt/task status where possible; otherwise reconcile by re-reading canonical state and enqueue a new, version-aware repair. At-least-once relays can duplicate delivery, so consumers must be idempotent.
- No assumed CAS: Meilisearch’s documented document APIs are asynchronous batch/indexing operations; its docs do not document a general per-document conditional “apply only if external version equals X” CAS. Therefore stale-write exclusion must be enforced in the producer/worker algorithm and repaired through reconciliation, not attributed to Meilisearch.
For a rebuild, create a shadow index for generation g+1g+1g+1, bulk-load a consistent database snapshot, replay/catch up all outbox changes after the snapshot watermark, validate count/sample/query health, then request the swap and record its task UID. Index swapping itself is asynchronous, although the completed swap exchanges documents, settings, and task history atomically. Only after the swap task succeeds should the active-generation pointer advance and cleanup be scheduled. On failure, retain the old live index, mark the generation failed, retain audit records, retry or rebuild a fresh shadow generation.
“Use source versions, watermarks, receipts, reconciliation, and generation pointers” is a local algorithmic inference built on those documented async/task semantics—not a claim that Meilisearch supplies end-to-end CAS or exactly-once indexing.

## C. Laravel packaging discipline

Split the integration into a framework-agnostic core plus an optional provider/package, for example:
- acme/search-core: contracts, PostgreSQL fallback, migrations/config abstractions; required dependencies only.
- acme/search-meilisearch: Meilisearch SDK binding and provider; explicitly installed only by consumers choosing that adapter.
Composer’s require means a dependency must be satisfiable for installation; suggest is informational and does not install a dependency. Thus put the optional SDK in the optional package’s require; put the optional adapter package in the core package’s suggest, with clear installation instructions.
Laravel service providers are container/resource registration points, and package discovery loads providers only for installed packages. Consequently, the core provider must not reference SDK classes, read provider secrets, create network clients, or validate Meilisearch credentials during boot. Bind fallback/default services lazily; the optional provider alone may bind the SDK client, and only when selected configuration requires it.
Conformance means testing a clean consumer install, not merely local development:
- Install only search-core with composer install --no-dev.
- Run config cache, route cache, queue worker startup, migrations, and representative fallback searches with no SDK/secrets.
- Separately install search-meilisearch, configure credentials, and run adapter/task/rebuild integration tests.
- Run composer validate; Composer documents that the schema is used by its validation command.
This separation makes “no engine installed” a supported production mode rather than an accidental boot-time failure.
